Heteromorphs and Prejudice.text: People whose Mutant Quirks give them visibly nonhuman bodies are called heteromorphs: animal heads, scales, stone skin, extra limbs, wings, tails. Cities have grown used to them. Some trains have wider doors and reinforced seats, clothing makers sell cuts for tails, wings and extra arms, and heteromorph pros can be national stars; Gang Orca, a top hero with the head and strength of an orca, is known across the country. Accommodation is still uneven: a uniform that does not fit, a helmet built only for a human head, a clinic without the right equipment, a public bath that turns away anyone with scales. Prejudice runs hardest in some isolated rural towns, where heteromorph children can be shunned, kept at home or blamed for bad luck, and adults who grew up that way often carry the scars long after they move away. In the cities the discrimination is quieter: an apartment that is suddenly taken when a heteromorph applicant arrives, a job interview that ends early, a stranger who changes seats on the train, an officer who questions the person with the frightening face first. Most heteromorphs want to be treated as individuals rather than as bodies. Many build ordinary lives, some turn their looks into an advantage in rescue or entertainment work, and a bitter few decide society will never accept them and stop trying. Activists push for better laws and design, and slurs that were common a generation ago now draw public criticism.
